What they share is that no person's token reaches either. The package answers "is this reachable by a human"; the scope answers "by which of us".

**`orgId` is in the body, not a header, and this is the only write on the platform surface where a caller names its own tenant.** Intelligence holds no session, so it has no active organisation to derive; a run happens for whichever tenant the work belonged to. That is safe only because `internal:intelligence` is issued to one service principal through client credentials and never to a browser client, so "the caller could name any organisation" describes a component we ship rather than an input a person controls. **If that scope ever reaches something a customer can drive, this becomes a tenancy hole.**

**Intelligence does not write this itself** because it holds no database credential (§1.6). Go persists; Python drafts and returns. The record travels back over this RPC, which also means it is written by something that can be trusted to report the org honestly.

**Called once, at the end.** There is no start call to pair with. A record its producer can amend afterwards is worth less than one it cannot, which is the argument `audit_log` rests on, and 00019 enforces it by granting update to nobody at all. The cost is that an in-flight run is invisible until it finishes; `queuedAt` is here from the start so ENT-238's queue wait is a subtraction rather than a migration.

**`AGENT_RUN_OUTCOME_REFUSED` is first class and is not a kind of failure.** §26.3 makes refusal what a working guardrail produces: a budget exhausted, a citation that did not resolve, an em dash the house style forbids, a tool outside the skill's allow-list. An enum with only success and failure would push refusals into one of them and lose the distinction that matters most for trust, which is "the harness stopped this" versus "the harness broke". `AGENT_RUN_OUTCOME_UNSPECIFIED` is refused rather than defaulted, because guessing would put a definite-looking value in the column a customer reads to decide whether to trust a finding.

**`citationsJson` carries both halves, and the rejected half is the important one.** A validator that silently dropped a bad citation would leave a record indistinguishable from a run where the model never tried to cite anything. The customer's question is "what did it get wrong", and an omission cannot answer it. This is not theoretical: asked three times which GDPR article requires a record of processing activities, the 2B tier answered 50, then 34, then 54. The answer is 30, and every response was schema-valid.

**`cachedInputTokens` is separate from `inputTokens`** because every provider offering prompt caching prices it separately, and because with a local model it is the measurement showing the corpus prefix is reused rather than reprocessed.

**`costMicros` is quoted**, being an int64 in proto3 JSON. Zero is the honest value for a local model rather than a missing one.

**Skill and model versions are required and refused when empty.** A run recorded without them answers "what produced this" with "something", which is worse than no row because it looks like an answer. For a local model, `modelVersion` is the weights' digest.

**`onBehalfOfUserId` is checked rather than believed, as of ENT-230.** It used to be written straight to the column, which meant a caller holding `internal:intelligence` could put any person's name on any run, in that person's own organisation's compliance record. Now a run that names somebody must also carry `delegation`, the credential core-api minted while serving that person's own request, and the two must agree; a run carrying no delegation must name nobody, which is what a scheduled sweep does. Both fields are empty in the body above for that reason: this request records a sweep.

**The delegation is EVIDENCE here and AUTHORITY nowhere else on this surface.** On the console requests it travels in the `Kindlast-Delegation` header and the request runs as the person. Recording a run is something the machine does as itself, on a scope no person holds, so it travels in the message instead. `orgId` must match the delegation's organisation too: a delegation is single-org, and a run recorded against another tenant is a caller bug rather than something to resolve silently.

Every refusal here is `permission_denied` with the same message, whether the delegation expired, was revoked, names somebody else or never existed. Four distinguishable answers would make this an oracle for which delegations are live.

The write runs on `kindlast_agent`, which holds insert and select on `agent_runs` and no update or delete. Minimal on purpose: §26.4's versioned profile reference and normalised evidence rows are ENT-228's, and `toolCallsJson` and `citationsJson` are jsonb precisely so that issue can normalise them without these columns changing meaning.

The Analyst, as an RPC. Required scope: `internal:intelligence`. **Served as of ENT-218.**

**A DIFFERENT SERVICE FROM EVERYTHING ELSE IN THIS COLLECTION.** This is Python, not core-api, which is why it has its own base URL. §1.6 splits the languages so Go loads and Go persists while Python drafts and returns, and this sits on the far side of that line: it holds no database credential, sets no tenancy GUC, and has no way to write a finding. The one thing it writes, it writes through core-api's `RecordAgentRun`.

**Use the client-credentials token.** No user token reaches this on any path. Two independent things enforce it: the audience is `kindlast-intelligence` and a human's console token carries a different one, and `internal:intelligence` is granted only to the machine user. That is not belt and braces: Intelligence has no tenancy GUCs and no RLS session, so it cannot check whether a human should see what it is processing. It never needs to, because a human cannot reach it.

**THE CALLER PASSES THE OBLIGATIONS, AND THEY ARE THE ONLY ONES THAT MAY BE CITED.** There is no fetch-them-yourself here and the absence is deliberate (§26.2). Inputs are what a skill needs before it starts and there is no decision in fetching them, so the caller assembles them in Go where the corpus is already readable. That keeps a run a pure function of its inputs, which is what makes it activity-shaped for Temporal at step 8.

The validator checks citations against **this list**, not against the corpus, and that is stronger than it sounds. A citation to an obligation that genuinely exists but is not in the list is still a fabrication: the model produced it from somewhere other than its context. Asking the corpus "does this exist" would have accepted it.

**A REFUSAL IS A 200, NOT AN ERROR.** §26.3 makes refusal what a working guardrail produces: a budget exhausted, a citation that did not resolve, a tool outside the allow-list. Returning `internal` for those would tell you the harness broke when it did exactly what it was built to do. Check `outcome`, not the status code.

**A refused narrative is not returned at all**, not even with a warning attached. `AGENTS.md` calls a fabricated citation worse than nothing, and handing a caller prose plus a note is how that prose reaches a customer.

**AN EM DASH OR EN DASH IN THE NARRATIVE IS ALSO A REFUSAL, AS OF ENT-163.** `AGENTS.md` forbids both characters in anything a customer reads. The system prompt has asked the model not to use them since ENT-160 and they kept arriving, which is the whole lesson: a prompt is a request, and only code refuses. `outcomeDetail` names the character, its position and the words around it, so a caller can tell this apart from a citation refusal without parsing anything. It refuses rather than substituting a comma, because a silent rewrite would edit a claim about the law with nobody as its author.

**`rejectedCitations` is the field to read when something looks wrong.** A response carrying only the good citations would be indistinguishable from a run where the model never tried to cite anything. This is not theoretical: asked three times which GDPR article requires a record of processing activities, the 2B tier answered 50, then 34, then 54. It is 30, and every answer was schema-valid.

**`agentRunId` is the row in `agent_runs`**, so a finding can point at the record of how it was made. Empty only when recording failed, and that case comes back as an error rather than a success: a narrative whose provenance was never stored is a finding nobody can check.

**`signal` is treated as data and never as instruction.** It reaches the model inside a fenced user message and never in the system prompt, because a compliance profile concatenated into a system prompt is a way to reprogram the Analyst.

**`delegation` is how a run acts for a person without this service ever holding a user token (ENT-230).** Minted by core-api, short lived, single-org, single-user and revocable. Intelligence cannot make one, cannot read inside one and cannot widen one; all it can do is hand it back, on `RecordAgentRun` and in the `Kindlast-Delegation` header of any tool call it makes. That is what keeps a machine principal from being able to act as whoever it names. Empty for a scheduled sweep, and empty here, because the Analyst declares no tools.

Draft narratives for findings that have none. Required scope: `internal:intelligence`. **Served as of ENT-245.**

**THE HALF ENT-218 ASSUMED AND NOBODY SCHEDULED.** ENT-218 shipped the harness, the guardrail ring, the citation validator and the `agent_runs` record, and nothing in the product called any of it. This is the call.

**A JOB, NOT PART OF THE SWEEP.** A model call inside the sweep's transaction would hold it open for minutes per finding on a local model, block the act path behind its locks, and lose everything on a timeout. The sweep stays fast and deterministic; this runs afterwards over findings that have no narrative. Latency and refusals become a queue's problem rather than a request's, which is also what makes it activity-shaped for Temporal at step 8.

**A NARRATIVE IS ADDED AND NEVER SUBSTITUTED.** It writes `findings.narrative`, `findings.agent_run_id` and `findings.narrative_generated_at`, and touches `detected`, `proposed_action`, `severity` and `status` not at all. The version that overwrote the sweep's text is ENT-164: model prose landed in `detected`, which the feed card renders as a heading, so a short phrase became a paragraph. Adding rather than overwriting means a refused run costs nothing and a deployment with no model is quieter rather than degraded.

**EACH RUN IS OFFERED EXACTLY ONE OBLIGATION: the finding's own.** The validator refuses any citation outside what was offered, so a narrative citing a different article is refused even when that article genuinely exists. This is the check that catches what the local model actually does: asked which GDPR article requires a record of processing activities, the 2B answered 50, then 34, then 54. It is 30. Offering the whole corpus would make that fabrication indistinguishable from a good citation.

**`intelligenceAvailable: false` IS A SUPPORTED ANSWER, NOT AN ERROR.** Intelligence sits behind the `model` compose profile, and `KINDLAST_INTELLIGENCE_URL` defaults to empty. A stack without it still produces findings with their deterministic text. “We have no model” and "the model is broken" want different reactions from an operator, so they are different responses.

**Read all four counts.** `narrated` plus `refused` plus `failed` should equal `attempted`. "3 of 10 narrated" is a different situation from "3 tried and 7 refused", and refusal is the guardrail working (§26.3) rather than a failure. A refusal is recorded on the finding so the next pass does not retry it forever, and so a customer can see that we tried and what was wrong with the answer.

**Runs are sequential.** One `llama-server` serves one request at a time, so firing these concurrently moves the queue rather than shortening it. Expect this to take minutes per finding on a local model.

**core-api NEEDS ITS OWN CREDENTIAL TO SERVE THIS, and the first version had none.** Intelligence declares `internal:intelligence` on `DraftNarrative` and refuses an unauthenticated call, so a core-api that sent no bearer token reported every finding as `failed` with “a bearer token is required”. Set `KINDLAST_INTERNAL_CLIENT_FILE` (the compose stack points it at the same `/machinekey/core-api-client.json` Intelligence reads, so both sides of the call are one credential rather than two that can drift) or `KINDLAST_INTERNAL_CLIENT_ID` and `KINDLAST_INTERNAL_CLIENT_SECRET`. Without it core-api warns at boot and answers `intelligenceAvailable: false`, because a narrator that cannot authenticate is not a degraded one, it is one that fails every call.

**Measured on the running stack, not assumed.** With the credential set, a seeded Article 30 finding narrated in about 40 seconds on the 2B tier, and `detected`, `proposed_action` and `status` were byte-identical afterwards.

What was decided, by whom, and when. Required scope: `audit:read`. **Served as of ENT-223.**

**This surface reads `audit_log` and nothing else.** Not traces, not model calls, not anything an observability tool holds (§7.2). That firewall is the product rather than an implementation detail: an auditor is buying a record a regulator can be shown, and a record assembled partly from a vendor's telemetry has completeness that depends on that vendor's retention settings. `audit_log` is append-only by trigger, lives in the customer's own database, and is written in the same transaction as the act it describes.

**Read only, and structurally so.** AuditService has no write RPC and will not get one. The table carries an append-only trigger, `kindlast_app` holds no update or delete grant on it, and the only insert path is bound by policy to the human in the GUC.

**No role gate**, unlike BillingService. Every member sees this, viewers included: a plan and a renewal date are commercial facts about the company, but "who approved this finding" is the shared record of the work these people did together. The organisation boundary is still absolute and supplied by RLS.

**There is no failure dimension and no `level` field**, which is the one real difference from the infrastructure log views this is modelled on. A refused act writes nothing, because the gates are constraints and policies and a refusal aborts the transaction the row would have been written in. Every row here is a thing that happened.

**`filter.until` is EXCLUSIVE.** Pulling January and then February with inclusive bounds returns any boundary row twice, and a duplicated decision in an audit file is a question nobody wants to have to answer. A range whose end is at or before its start is `invalid_argument` rather than swapped or ignored: both of those look like they worked, and in an export the difference is a month of decisions versus all of them.

**`filter.query` does not search `before` and `after`.** Those hold whatever the acted-on row contained, which for a DSAR includes a data subject's name, and a substring search across them would turn the audit log into a search engine over the personal data it exists to account for. It searches the action type, the target table, and the actor's name and email. The payloads are still returned in full: it is the search that stops at the boundary, not the record.

**`actor.actorRole` is the role held AT THE TIME**, snapshotted into the row rather than resolved now. A client that looked it up would relabel a past act every time somebody's role changed. `actor.displayName` and `actor.email` are empty for an actor who has left, and the row is still returned: a log that dropped entries when somebody was offboarded would be defeatable by offboarding somebody.

**`agentRunId` and `actor.kind` are declared and always unpopulated.** `agent_runs` arrives with ENT-218 (§26). They exist now so the day an agent produces an act is a server change rather than a contract change, and so nothing gets written on the assumption that every actor is a human.

Pagination is keyset over `(occurred_at desc, id desc)`. The id tie-break matters more here than in the other registers: an act writes the decision and the record it created in ONE transaction, so both rows share `occurred_at` exactly, and without it a cursor skips a row or repeats one forever. `pageToken` is opaque; `pageSize` defaults to 50 and caps at 200.

`availableActionTypes` lists every action type present in this organisation's log, ignoring the filter, so a console can offer only values that would return something.

The same filtered set, as a file an auditor can attach to a report. Required scope: `audit:read`. **Served as of ENT-223.**

**A separate RPC rather than a flag on the list**, because the two answer different questions. The list answers "what is on this page" and is paged by construction. This answers "everything that matched", and an export that silently stopped at a page boundary is worse than none: the auditor cannot see the truncation, and the file is the artefact that leaves the building.

**Check `truncated` on every response.** It is true when the export hit its 50,000 row cap, and it is the only signal there is: a truncated CSV is a valid CSV that simply stops. `rowCount` says how many rows the file holds. Narrow the range and export again.

**The response is a `oneof` and today it is always `content`.** §7 designs the export as a request returning a signed download URL and §25 leaves synchronous-versus-job open. A synchronous body is right at today's volumes; the shape that grows into a URL is decided now, so the day a customer's log outgrows one response it becomes `download` with no contract break and no second RPC. **The synchronous path is the interim, not the decision.**

`content.data` is base64 over Connect's JSON codec, which is how proto `bytes` travel. Decode it before writing the file.

**The file carries a UTF-8 BOM**, for the unglamorous reason that Excel on Windows otherwise reads UTF-8 as the local code page and mangles every non-ASCII name. The names that get mangled are disproportionately not English ones, and this is a record of who did what.

**Spreadsheet formula injection is defused.** Any cell opening with `= + - @` or a leading tab is prefixed with an apostrophe, OWASP's mitigation. Several columns carry text a user chose (a display name, and the `before`/`after` payloads), the person opening the file is an auditor on a corporate laptop, and spreadsheets evaluate those cells. **This changes the exported bytes deliberately**: the record of truth is `audit_log` in the customer's own database, untouched and append-only, and a rendering that can execute is not a safer record. A parser consuming these files should strip a single leading apostrophe.

**The column order is a contract.** Somebody will point a spreadsheet at column C. Append, never rearrange: `occurred_at, action_type, actor_user_id, actor_name, actor_email, actor_role, finding_id, target_table, target_id, before, after, agent_run_id, audit_id`.

Timestamps are RFC 3339 in UTC, not a friendly local format. This file is read in other timezones and possibly years later, and `14:32` with no offset is a fact nobody can verify.

**`format` may be omitted**, and UNSPECIFIED is accepted as CSV. It is the only format there is, so refusing an unset enum would fail every caller written against the obvious reading of a one-value enum. A second format changes that.

A zero-row export is a real answer and still returns a file with its header row: a completely empty file reads as a broken download.

`web`'s download endpoint, in front of ExportAuditEntries. **Implemented as of ENT-223.**

In the collection because it is one of the halves that will never appear in a proto file: a browser-facing route with its own status codes and its own headers, which is exactly what this collection is the source of truth for.

**Authenticated by the session cookie, not a bearer token**, so this request only works from a browser that has signed in. There is nothing to paste into Postman here; it is documented so the contract is reviewable.

**A route handler rather than a server action**, because the result is a file and a download has to survive being a plain link. A server action returning bytes needs client-side JavaScript to turn them into a saved file, and the artefact an auditor's whole workflow ends in should not depend on a hydration step.

It reads the SAME query string the page does, through the same `toFilter`, which is what makes "export what I am looking at" true by construction rather than because two implementations agree. `page` is deliberately dropped: an export is the whole matching set, and carrying a cursor into it would be asking for "everything, starting from page three".

**The filename carries the truncation.** When core-api reports the cap was hit, the file is named `-partial`. That is the only signal that survives the trip: the file gets attached to a report and emailed onwards long after any banner in the console is gone, and a name is the one piece of context that travels with it. `X-Kindlast-Truncated` and `X-Kindlast-Row-Count` carry the same facts for a script.

Status codes worth knowing: **401** with no session, and deliberately not a redirect, because redirecting a file endpoint into a sign-in page saves an HTML document called `audit.csv`. **404** for a slug the caller does not belong to, matching the rest of the console, so this cannot be used to discover which organisations exist. **400** when core-api refused the filter (a backwards range). **502** when core-api was unreachable or returned no file; a response with no content is a fault rather than an empty export, because an export of nothing still carries a header row and a zero-byte file looks like an answer.

`Cache-Control: no-store, private`. This is a per-organisation record behind a session, and a shared proxy holding one tenant's audit log is the worst cache bug available in this product.
